def f(n: Int) : Int =
  if n < 0 then this.g(n) else n
end f

def g(n: Int) : Int =
  this.f(n+1)
end g

end A

class B extends A:
  override def f(n: Int) : Int =
    super.f(n) + 1
  end f

  override def g(n: Int) : Int =
    this.f(-n)
  end g

end B

    def f(n: Int) : Int =
        this.f(n+1)
    end f
end A

class B extends A:
    override def f(n: Int) : Int =
        if n < 0 then super.f(n) else n
    end f

    def g(n: Int) : Int =
        this.f(-n)
    end g
end B

a.g(-5)

class A:
    def f(n: Int) : Int =
        this.f(n+1)
    end f
end A

class B extends A:
    override def f(n: Int) : Int =
        if n < 0 then super.f(n) else n
    end f

    def g(n: Int) : Int =
        this.f(-n)
    end g
end B

Code:
public class MyArray {
    public int[] elems // ...
    public MyArray map(IntMapper m) {
        MyArray result = new MyArray();
        for (int i = 0; i < elems.length; i++) {
            result.elems[i] = m.apply(elems[i]);
        }
        return result;
    }
}

Type: slide, code

Content:
Title: "Higher-order functions" in Java 1.0

Left:
```java
public class MyArray {
    public int[] elems // ...
    public MyArray map(IntMapper m) {
        MyArray result = new MyArray();
        for (int i = 0; i < elems.length; i++) {
            result.elems[i] = m.apply(elems[i]);
        }
        return result;
    }
}
```

Right:
```java
interface IntMapper {
    public int apply(int v);
}
class IntIncrement implements IntMapper {
    public int apply(int v) {
        return v + 1;
    }
}
```

Bottom:
```java
public static void main(String[] args) {
    MyArray a = new MyArray();
    // fill a
    // passing in an instance of a named class
    MyArray b = a.map(new IntIncrement());
}
```

Type: slide, code

Content:
Title: "Higher-order functions" in Java 1.0

Left:
```java
public class MyArray {
    public int[] elems // ...
    public MyArray map(IntMapper m) {
        MyArray result = new MyArray();
        for (int i = 0; i < elems.length; i++) {
            result.elems[i] = m.apply(elems[i]);
        }
        return result;
    }
}
```

Right:
```java
interface IntMapper {
    public int apply(int v);
}
class IntIncrement implements IntMapper {
    public int apply(int v) {
        return v + 1;
    }
}
```

Type: slide, code

Content:
Title: "Higher-order functions" in Java 1.0

Left:
```java
public class MyArray {
    public int[] elems // ...
    public MyArray map(IntMapper m) {
        MyArray result = new MyArray();
        for (int i = 0; i < elems.length; i++) {
            result.elems[i] = m.apply(elems[i]);
        }
        return result;
    }
}
```

Right:
```java
interface IntMapper {
    public int apply(int v);
}
class IntIncrement implements IntMapper {
    public int apply(int v) {
        return v + 1;
    }
}
```

Top: Java Functional Interface

Bullet points:
- java.util.function defines many functional interfaces
- Also java.awt.event, Runnable, Callable, etc

Code blocks:
1. @FunctionalInterface
   interface Function<T,R> {
       public R apply (T x);
   }

2. Function<Integer,Integer> intIncrement = new Function<>() {
       public Integer apply (Integer x) { return x + 1; }
   };

3. Function<Integer,Integer> intIncrement = x -> x + 1;

~/tmp

Your bash commands will be sandboxed. Disable with /sandbox.

Code:
xs = ["10", "10", "10"];
xs.map(parseInt) /* [10, NaN, 2] */ ... why!?

• Array.map passes three arguments to its callback: (element, index, array).
parseInt accepts two: (string, radix).

So what actually executes is:
parseInt("10", 0)  // radix 0 → treated as base 10 → 10
parseInt("10", 1)  // radix 1 → invalid → NaN

Type: code

Content:
Top: Understand parseInt behavi
Your bash commands will be sandboxed. Disable with /sandbox.

Code:
xs = ["10", "10", "10"];
xs.map(parseInt) /* [10, NaN, 2] */ ... why!?

• Array.map passes three arguments to its callback: (element, index, array).
parseInt accepts two: (string, radix).

So what actually executes is:
parseInt("10", 0)  // radix 0 → treated as base 10 → 10
parseInt("10", 1)  // radix 1 → invalid → NaN
parseInt("10", 2)  // radix 2 → binary "10" → 2

Fix: Wrap it so only the element is passed:
xs.map(x => parseInt(x, 10))  // [10, 10, 10]

Bottom: esc to interrupt

Type: code

Content:
Top: Understand parseInt beha

Code:
xs = ["10", "10", "10"];
xs.map(parseInt) /* [10, NaN, 2] */ // ... why?

• Array.map passes three arguments to its callback: (element, index, array).
parseInt accepts two: (string, radix).

So what actually executes is:
parseInt("10", 0)  // radix 0 → treated as base 10 → 10
parseInt("10", 1)  // radix 1 → invalid          → NaN
parseInt("10", 2)  // radix 2 → binary "10"     → 2

Fix: Wrap it so only the element is passed:
xs.map(x => parseInt(x, 10))  // [10, 10, 10]

Or use Number:
xs.map(Number)  // [10, 10, 10] - Number only takes one arg anyway

Center:
  Title: Closures
  Text: A closure is the combination of a function bundled together (enclosed) with references to its surrounding state (the lexical environment). In other words, a closure gives a function access to its outer scope. In JavaScript, closures are created every time a function is created, at function creation time.

  Subtitle: Lexical scoping
  Text: Consider the following example code:
  Code: JS
    function init() {
      // code

Content:
Top: 
A closure is the combination of a function bundled together (enclosed) with references to its surrounding state (the lexical environment). In other words, a closure gives a function access to its outer scope. In JavaScript, closures are created every time a function is created, at function creation time.

Left:
- Equality comparisons and sameness
- Enumerability and ownership of properties
- Closures
  - Advanced
- References
  - Built-in objects
  - Expressions & operators
  - Statements & declarations
  - Functions

Center:
Heading: Lexical scoping
Text: Consider the following example code:

Code:
```javascript
function init() {
  var name = "Mozilla"; // name is a local variable created by init
  function displayName() {
    // displayName() is the inner function, that forms a closure
    console.log(name); // use variable declared in the parent function
  }
}
```

Title: Functional Programming

Bullet points:
• Functions and objects are first-class citizens
  ○ create at runtime
  ○ pass as args, return, store in data structures
• Nested functions (and objects) are commonplace: callbacks, collections processing
• JS uses static (lexical) scoping, see here

Title: Functional Programming

============================================================
时间戳: 01:27:31 (5251.00s), OCR耗时: 1.74s, 平均耗时: 1.48s, InputTokens: 1397, OutputTokens: 192
============================================================
Type: slide, code

Content:
Title: Recursion: Tail-Call Optimization

Bullet Points:
- JavaScript standard includes tail-call optimization, but only Safari implements it
- Can still make sense to think about alternative implementations

Left Code Block:
```javascript
function fib(n) {
  if (n==0) return 0;
  else if (n==1) return 1;
  else return fib(n-2) + fib(n-1);
}
```

Right Code Block:
```javascript
function fibtail(n) {
  // nested function, inner n shadows outer n
  function fibtail(n, r1, r2) {
    if (n==0) return r1;
    else if (n==1) return r2;
    else return fibtail(n-1, r2, r1+r2);
  }
  return fibtail(n, 0, 1);
}
```

  else if (n==1) return 1;
  else return fib(n-2) + fib(n-1);
}
```

Right Code:
```javascript
function fibtail(n) {
  // nested function, inner n shadows outer n
  function fibtail(n, r1, r2) {
    if (n==0) return r1;
    else if (n==1) return r2;
    else return fibtail(n-1, r2, r1+r2);
  }
  return fibtail(n, 0, 1);
}
```

Content:
Title: Static (Lexical) Scope with Hoisting

Left:
- Variables var are function-scoped
  • Hoists variable declarations to top of nearest enclosing function
  • Initialization code is not hoisted

Code (Left):
```javascript
var a = 1;
function f () {
  console.log ("f1: a = " + a); // a=undefined
  {
    var a = 2;
    console.log ("f2: a = " + a); // a=2
  }
}
function main() {
  console.log ("m1: a = " + a); // a=1
  f ();
  console.log ("m2: a = " + a); // a=1
}
```

Right:
- Equivalent code: variable declared at top of function
- Initialization code remains in place

    console.log ("f2: a = " + a); // a=2
  }
}

}

时间戳: 01:30:19 (5419.00s), OCR耗时: 0.00s, 平均耗时: 1.47s, InputTokens: 0, OutputTokens: 0
============================================================
Type: code

Content:
Top: Understand parseInt beha

Code:
xs = ["10", "10", "10"];
xs.map(parseInt) /* [10, NaN, 2] */ ... why?

• Array.map passes three arguments to its callback: (element, index, array).
parseInt accepts two: (string, radix).

So what actually executes is:
parseInt("10", 0)  // radix 0 → treated as base 10 → 10
parseInt("10", 1)  // radix 1 → invalid → NaN
parseInt("10", 2)  // radix 2 → binary "10" → 2

Fix: Wrap it so only the element is passed:
xs.map(x => parseInt(x, 10))  // [10, 10, 10]

Or use Number:
xs.map(Number)  // [10, 10, 10] - Number only takes one arg anyway

Bottom: * Churned for 7s
> |
? for shortcuts · < for agents

Type: slide, code

Content:
Title: Argument Passing and Pattern Matching

Bullet Points:
- Call by value, but objects and arrays are references (changes to fields or elements)
- Pattern matching for arrays
  Code:
  ```javascript
  function swaparray(a) {
    const [x,y] = a; // deconstruct array
    a[0] = y;
    a[1] = x;
  }
  ```
- Swap array
  Code:
  ```javascript
  let a = [1, 2, 3, 4];
  swaparray(a); // a === [2, 1, 3, 4]
  ```
- Swap in place
  Code:
  ```javascript
  let x = 1, y = 2;
  [y,x] = [x,y];
  ```
- Pattern matching for objects
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const person = {
    name: "Alice",
    age: 50,
    addr: "243 S Wabash"
  }
  ```
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const { name, _, addr } = person
  ```
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const { name } = person
  ```
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const { n, _1, _2, o } = person
  ```

Type: slide, code

Content:
Title: Argument Passing and Pattern Matching

Bullet Points:
- Call by value, but objects and arrays are references (changes to fields or elements)
- Pattern matching for arrays
  Code:
  ```javascript
  function swaparray(a) {
    const [x,y] = a; // deconstruct array
    a[0] = y;
    a[1] = x;
  }
  ```
- Swap array
  Code:
  ```javascript
  let a = [1, 2, 3, 4];
  swaparray(a); // a === [2, 1, 3, 4]
  ```
- Swap in place
  Code:
  ```javascript
  let x = 1, y = 2;
  [y,x] = [x,y];
  ```
- Pattern matching for objects
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const person = {
    name: "Alice",
    age: 50,
    addr: "243 S Wabash"
  }
  ```
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const { name, _, addr } = person
  ```
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const { name } = person
  ```
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const { n, _1, _2, o } = person
  ```

  Code:
  ```javascript
  const person = {

  }

  Code:

  ```javascript

  ```

  ```javascript

  ```

Title: Argument Passing and Pattern Matching

Bullet Points:
- Call by value, but objects and arrays are references (changes to fields or elements)
- Pattern matching for arrays
  Code:
  ```javascript
  function swaparray(a) {
    const [x,y] = a; // deconstruct array
    a[0] = y;
    a[1] = x;
  }
  ```
- Swap array
  Code:
  ```javascript
  let a = [1, 2, 3, 4];
  swaparray(a); // a === [2, 1, 3, 4]
  ```
- Swap in place
  Code:
  ```javascript
  let x = 1, y = 2;
  [y,x] = [x,y];
  ```
- Pattern matching for objects
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const person = {
    name: "Alice",
    age: 50,
    addr: "243 S Wabash"
  }
  ```
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const { name, _, addr } = person
  ```
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const { name } = person
  ```
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const { n, _1, _2, o } = person
  ```

  swaparray(a); // a === [2, 1, 3, 4]
  ```
- Swap in place
  Code:
  ```javascript
  let x = 1, y = 2;
  [y,x] = [x,y];
  ```
- Pattern matching for objects
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const person = {
    name: "Alice",
    age: 50,
    addr: "243 S Wabash"
  }
  ```
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const { name, _, addr } = person
  ```
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const { name } = person
  ```
  Code:
  ```javascript
  const { n, _1, _2, o } = person
  ```

• With lambda expressions (=>)
Code:
1 var xs = [ 11, 21, 31 ];
2
3 xs.map (x => (2 * x));
4 xs.filter (x => x%7===0);
5 xs.reduce ((z,x) => z+x, 0);

Right:
• With functions
Code:
1 var xs = [ 11, 21, 31 ];
2
3 xs.map (function(x) { return (2 * x); });
4 xs.filter (function(x) { return x%7===0 });
5 xs.reduce (function(z,x) { return z+x; }, 0);

• Beware: return mandatory, outer this not closed

Top: Closures

Left:
• Recall: Java requires effectively-final i from enclosing scope
Code:
1 for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
2     int x = i; /* accepted: x effectively final */
3     new Thread (new Runnable () {
4         public void run () {
5             while (true) { System.out.print (x); }
6         }
7     }).start ();
8 }

Right:
• JS allows shared i; unwanted effect with var

1 var funcs = [];
2 for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
3     funcs.push (function () { return i; });
4 }
5 funcs.map (f => f());
6 // [ 5, 5, 5, 5, 5 ]

• Fix with var similar to Java?

1 var funcs = [];

• Beware: hoisting!

Right:
• Use block-scoped let or const
Code:
1 let funcs = [];
2 for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
3   const x = i; /* block scope */
4   funcs.push (function () { return x; });
5 }
6 funcs.map (f => f());
7 // [ 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 ]

3   var x = i;
4   funcs.push (function () { return x; });
5 }
6 funcs.map (f => f());
7 // [ 4, 4, 4, 4, 4 ]
• Beware: hoisting!

Right:
• Use block-scoped let or const
Code:
1 let funcs = [];
2 for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
3   const x = i; /* block scope */
4   funcs.push (function () { return x; });
5 }
6 funcs.map (f => f());
7 // [ 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 ]

Heading: JavaScript
Text:
JavaScript (JS) is a lightweight interpreted (or just-in-time compiled) programming language with first-class functions. While it is most well-known as the scripting language for Web pages, many non-browser environments also use it, such as Node.js, Apache CouchDB and Adobe Acrobat. JavaScript is a prototype-based, garbage-collected, dynamic language, supporting multiple paradigms such as imperative, functional, and object-oriented.

JavaScript's dynamic capabilities include runtime object construction, variable parameter lists, function variables, dynamic script creation (via eval), object introspection (via for...in and Object utilities), and source-code recovery (JavaScript functions store their source text and can be retrieved through toString()).

Top: 5 JavaScript "Bad" Parts That Are Fixed In ES6 - Google Chrome
Title: 5 JavaScript "Bad" Parts That Are Fixed In ES6
By: rajaraodv

Text:
ECMAScript 6 (ES6) features can be divided into features that are pure syntactic sugar (like: class), features that enhance JavaScript (like import) and features that fix some of JavaScript's "bad" parts (like the let keyword). Most blogs and articles combine all three types, and can overwhelm newcomers. So I'm writing this post that focuses on just the key ES6 features that fix "bad" parts.

I hope that by the end of this blog you'll realize that by using just a couple ES6 features like let and the fat-arrow, you'll get massive returns.

OK, Let's get started.

3. var counter2 = { n: 0, get () { return this.n++; } };

Bullet 2: Invoke the functions
Code:
1. > [counter1.get(), counter2.get()]
2. [0, 0]

Bullet 3: Access the functions
Code:
1. > [counter1.get, counter2.get]
2. [ [Function: get],
3.   [Function: get] ]

Type: slide, code

Content:
Title: Object Literals

Left:
• Objects have properties
Code:
1 var empty = {}; /* Object literal with no contents */
2 var person = { /* Object literal with three properties */
3   name: "Alice",
4   age: 50,
5   addr: "243 S Wabash Ave"
6 };

• Access properties
Code:
1 > person.name
2 'Alice'
3 > person.name.length
4 5

Right:
• Update properties
Code:
1 > person.age = person.age + 1
2 51

• Access undefined property
Code:
1 > person.occupation
2 undefined

Right: Scala
Code:
1 object o { var n = -1; def next() = { this.n += 1; this.n } }
2 var fNext = o.next _
3 fNext() // 0: closure binds this to o

Bullet points:
• Scala Methods are not Functions
• In Scala, this is closed when converting method to function

Ok this was going to be a short post that I could link to when people get confused on #scala, but it turns out that there are a lot of cases to consider. It would be nice if this could just be the last word on methods vs. functions in Scala, so if I missed anything please let me know.

TL;DR ... Methods in Scala are not values, but functions are. You can construct a function that delegates to a method via η-expansion (triggered by the trailing underscore thingy).

Text:
The definition I will be using here is that a method is something defined with def and a value is something you can assign to a val.

Heading: The Basic Idea
Text: When we define a method we see that we cannot assign it to a val.

Code:
scala> def add1(n: Int): Int = n + 1
add1: (n: Int)Int

scala> val f = add1
<console>:8: error: missing arguments for method add1;
follow this method with '_' if you want to treat it as a partially applied function
val f = add1

============================================================
时间戳: 02:12:56 (7976.00s), OCR耗时: 2.54s, 平均耗时: 1.76s, InputTokens: 1397, OutputTokens: 307

Type: webpage, code

Content:
Top: 
tpolecat.github.io/2014/06/09/methods-functions.html

Left:
scala> def add1(n: Int): Int = n + 1
add1: (n: Int)Int

scala> val f = add1
<console>:8: error: missing arguments for method add1;
follow this method with '_' if you want to treat it as a partially applied function
val f = add1
^

Note also the type of add1, which doesn't look normal; you can't declare a variable of type (n: Int)Int. Methods are not values.

However, by adding the η-expansion postfix operator (η is pronounced "eta"), we can turn the method into a function value. Note the type of f.

scala> val f = add1 _
f: Int => Int = <function1>

scala> f(3)
res0: Int = 4

The effect of _ is to perform the equivalent of the following: we construct a Function1 instance that delegates to our method.

scala> val g = new Function1[Int, Int] { def apply(n: Int): Int = add1(n) }
g: Int => Int = <function1>

scala> g(3)
res18: Int = 4

So that's really all there is to it. The rest of this post is just details.

Bottom:
Automatic Expansion

Top: 
So that's really all there is to it. The rest of this post is just details.

Heading: Automatic Expansion
In contexts where the compiler expects a function type, the desired expansion is inferred and the underscore is not needed:

Code:
scala> List(1,2,3).map(add1 _)
res5: List[Int] = List(2, 3, 4)

scala> List(1,2,3).map(add1)
res6: List[Int] = List(2, 3, 4)

Text: This applies in any position where a function type is expected, as is the case with a declared or ascribed type:

Code:
scala> val z = add1
<console>:8: error: missing arguments for method add1;
follow this method with '_' if you want to treat it as a partially applied function
val z = add1
^

scala> val z: Int => Int = add1
z: Int => Int = <function1>

scala> val z = add1: Int => Int
z: Int => Int = <function1>

Heading: Effect of Overloading
In the presence of overloading you must provide enough type information to disambiguate:

Left:
- Effect of Overloading
  In the presence of overloading you must provide enough type information to disambiguate:
  Code:
    scala> "foo".substring _
    <console>: error: ambiguous reference to overloaded definition,
    both method substring in class String of type (x$1: Int, x$2: Int)String
    and method substring in class String of type (x$1: Int)String
    match expected type ?
    "foo".substring _
    scala> "foo".substring _ : (Int => String)
    res14: Int => String = <function1>

- Fistful of Parameters
  Scala actually has a lot of ways to specify parameters, but they all work with η-expansion. Let's look at each case.

    Methods with no parameter list follow the same pattern, but in this case the compiler can't tell us about the missing _ because the invocation is legal on its own.

============================================================
Type: webpage

Content:
Top: Fistful of Parameters
Text: Scala actually has a lot of ways to specify parameters, but they all work with η-expansion. Let's look at each case.

Heading: Parameterless Methods
Text: Methods with no parameter list follow the same pattern, but in this case the compiler can't tell us about the missing _ because the invocation is legal on its own.

Code:
scala> def x = println("hi")
x: Unit

scala> val z = x // ok
hi
z: Unit = {}

scala> val z = x _
z: () => Unit = <function0>

scala> z()
hi

Text: Note that unlike the method (which has no parameter list) the function value has an empty parameter list.

Heading: Multiple Parameters
Text: Methods with multiple parameters expand to equivalent multi-parameter functions:

Code:
scala> def plus(a: Int, b: Int): Int = a + b
plus: (a: Int, b: Int)Int

Title: Binding this

Left: JavaScript
Code:
```javascript
var o = { n: -1, next () { this.n += 1; return this.n; } };
var fNext = o.next
fNext() // NaN: closure does not bind this to o
```
Bullet points:
- JS methods are properties that hold functions
- In JS, this is not bound in the closure

Right: Scala
Code:
```scala
object o { var n = -1; def next() = { this.n += 1; this.n } }
var fNext = o.next
fNext() // 0: closure binds this to o
```
Bullet points:
- Scala Methods are not Functions
- In Scala, this is closed when converting method to function

时间戳: 02:15:16 (8116.00s), OCR耗时: 2.21s, 平均耗时: 1.76s, InputTokens: 1397, OutputTokens: 220
============================================================
Type: slide, code

Content:
Top: Binding this

Left:
What is wrong below?
Code:
1 var o = {
2   v : 5,
3   add : function (xs) {
4     return xs.map(function(x) {
5       return this.v + x;
6     });
7   }
8 }
9 o.add([10,20,30]) // [ NaN, NaN, NaN ]

Bullet:
• Inside map is function context, so this refers to global/window

Right:
• Before EcmaScript5 fix: alias this
Code:
1 var o = {
2   v : 5,
3   add : function (xs) {
4     var me = this;
5     return xs.map(function(x){ return me.v + x; });
6   }
7 }
8 o.add([10,20,30]) // [ 15, 25, 35 ]

Bullet:
• Outside map but inside add is method context, so this refers to o

Bottom right: 13

Type: slide, code, diagram

Content:
Top: Creating Objects

Bullet points:
• Call function using new: constructor context
• Binds this to newly created object inside function

Left:
Code:
1 function Counter () {
2   this.n = -1;
3   this.next = function () { return ++this.n; }
4 }

Code:
1 var c1 = new Counter (); // Constructor context
2 var c2 = new Counter ();
3 [c1.next(), c1.next(), c2.next(), c1.next()] // [ 0, 1, 0, 2 ]

Right:
Diagram:
Shows two objects c1 and c2, each with n = -1.
Each has a next method (function) that returns ++this.n.
Connections show prototype chain: c1 and c2 → Counter → Function.
Labels: return ++this.n; for both next methods.

Code:
1 var cx = Counter (); // Function context!
2 cx.next() // Uncaught TypeError:
3 // cx is undefined (no return in Counter)
4 // instead, window now has properties n and next
5 [window.next(), window.next()] // [ 0, 1 ]

Title: Creating Objects

Bullet Points:
- Call function using new: constructor context
- Binds this to newly created object inside function

Code (Left):
```javascript
function Counter () {
  this.n = -1;
  this.next = function () { return ++this.n; }
}
```

Code (Bottom Left):
```javascript
var c1 = new Counter (); // Constructor context
var c2 = new Counter ();
[c1.next(), c1.next(), c2.next(), c1.next()] // [0, 1, 0, 2]
```

Code (Right):
```javascript
var cx = Counter (); // Function context!
cx.next() // Uncaught TypeError:
// cx is undefined (no return in Counter)
// instead, window now has properties n and next
[window.next(), window.next()] // [0, 1]
```

Diagram (Top Right):
- Shows object creation with `new`
- Two objects: c1 (n=-1) and c2 (n=-1)
- Each has a `next` method returning ++this.n
- Prototype chain: Counter → Function → Object
- Arrows indicate method calls and prototype inheritance
- Labels: "return ++this.n" for next method

  this.n = -1;
  this.next = function () { return ++this.n; }
}

Code:
var c1 = new Counter (); // Constructor context
var c2 = new Counter ();
[c1.next(), c1.next(), c2.next()] // [0, 1, 0, 2]

Right:
Code:
var cx = Counter (); // Function context!
cx.next() // Uncaught TypeError:
// cx is undefined (no return in Counter)
// Instead, window now has properties n and next
[window.next(), window.next()] // [0, 1]

Diagram:
Shows object creation with prototype chain:
- c1 and c2 objects with n = -1
- Each has next method returning ++this.n
- Prototype links to Counter constructor
- Function context (cx) leads to window object pollution

Content:
Title: Creating Objects

Bullet Points:
- Call function using new: constructor context
- Binds this to newly created object inside function

Code (Left):
```javascript
function Counter () {
  this.n = -1;
  this.next = function () { return ++this.n; }
}
```

Code (Right):
```javascript
var cx = Counter(); // Function context!
cx.next() // Uncaught TypeError:
// cx is undefined (no return in Counter)
// instead, window now has properties n and next
[window.next(), window.next()] // [0, 1]
```

Code (Bottom Left):
```javascript
var c1 = new Counter(); // Constructor context
var c2 = new Counter();
[c1.next(), c1.next(), c2.next(), c1.next()] // [0, 1, 0, 2]
```

Diagram:
- Shows object creation with `new Counter()`
- Two objects: c1 (n=-1) and c2 (n=-1)
- Each has a `next` method that increments `n`
- `this` is bound to the object instance
- `proto` links to `Counter` constructor
- `Function` links to `next` method
- `return ++this.n;` shown for method execution
- `cx = Counter()` leads to `window` gaining properties `n` and `next`

function Counter () {
  this.n = -1;
  this.next = function () { return ++this.n; }

```

Diagram (Top Right):
- Shows object creation with `new`
- Two objects: c1 (n=-1) and c2 (n=-1)
- Each has a `next` method returning ++this.n
- Prototype chain: Counter → Function → Object
- Arrows indicate method calls and prototype inheritance
- Labels: "return ++this.n" for next method

function Counter () {

- Labels: "return ++this.n" for next method

```

- Prototype chain: Counter → Function → Object
- Arrows indicate method calls and prototype inheritance

Type: slide, code, diagram

Content:
Top: Creating Objects

Bullet points:
• Call function using new: constructor context
• Binds this to newly created object inside function

Code (Left):
1 function Counter () {
2   this.n = -1;
3   this.next = function () { return ++this.n; }
4 }

Code (Middle):
1 var c1 = new Counter (); // Constructor context
2 var c2 = new Counter ();
3 [c1.next(), c1.next(), c2.next(), c1.next()] // [ 0, 1, 0, 2 ]

Code (Right):
1 var cx = Counter (); // Function context!
2 cx.next() // Uncaught TypeError:
3 // cx is undefined (no return in Counter)
4 // instead, window now has properties n and next
5 [window.next(), window.next()] // [ 0, 1 ]

Bottom: Every object has own set of methods c1.next != c2.next

Diagram (Right side):
Shows two objects c1 and c2, each with n = -1.
Each has a next method (function) that returns ++this.n.
c1 and c2 both link to a Counter prototype, which links to a Function prototype.
The diagram illustrates the prototype chain and method binding.

Code (Middle):
1 var c1 = new Counter (); // Constructor context
2 var c2 = new Counter ();
3 [c1.next(), c1.next(), c2.next(), c1.next()] // [ 0, 1, 0, 2 ]

Code (Right):
1 var cx = Counter (); // Function context!
2 cx.next() // Uncaught TypeError:
3 // cx is undefined (no return in Counter)
4 // instead, window now has properties n and next
5 [window.next(), window.next()] // [ 0, 1 ]

Bottom: Every object has own set of methods c1.next != c2.next

Diagram (Right side):
Shows two objects c1 and c2, each with n = -1.
Each has a next method (function) that returns ++this.n.
c1 and c2 both link to a Counter prototype, which links to a Function prototype.
The diagram illustrates the prototype chain and method binding.

Top: Creating Objects

• Call function using new: constructor context
• Binds this to newly created object inside function

Code (Left):
1 function Counter () {
2   this.n = -1;
3   this.next = function () { return ++this.n; }
4 }

1 var c1 = new Counter (); // Constructor context
2 var c2 = new Counter ();
3 [c1.next(), c1.next(), c2.next(), c1.next()] // [ 0, 1, 0, 2 ]

1 var cx = Counter (); // Function context!
2 cx.next() // Uncaught TypeError:
3 // cx is undefined (no return in Counter)
4 // instead, window now has properties n and next
5 [window.next(), window.next()] // [ 0, 1 ]

Bottom: Every object has own set of methods c1.next != c2.next

Diagram (Right side):
Shows two objects c1 and c2, each with n = -1.
Each has a next method (function) that returns ++this.n.
c1 and c2 both link to a Counter prototype, which links to a Function prototype.
The diagram illustrates the prototype chain and method binding.

Center:
  Title: Inheritance and the prototype chain
  Text: In programming, inheritance refers to passing down characteristics from a parent to a child so that a new piece of code can reuse and build upon the features of an existing one. JavaScript implements inheritance by using objects. Each object has an internal link to another object called its prototype. That prototype object has a prototype of its own, and so on until an object is reached with null as its prototype. By definition, null has no prototype and acts as the final link in this prototype chain. It is possible to mutate any member of the prototype chain or even swap out the prototype at runtime, so concepts like static dispatching do not exist in JavaScript.
  Text: JavaScript is a bit confusing for developers experienced in class-based languages (like Java or C++), as it is dynamic and does not have static types. While this confusion is often considered to be one of JavaScript’s weaknesses, the prototypical inheritance model itself

Title: Delegation-based Inheritance

    - Mozilla
    - JavaScript Core

  - Only functions have prototype

```java
public class MyArray {
    public int[] elems // ...
    public MyArray map(IntMapper m) {
        MyArray result = new MyArray();

Title: "Higher-order functions" in Java 1.0

Left:
```java
public class MyArray {
    public int[] elems // ...
    public MyArray map(IntMapper m) {
        MyArray result = new MyArray();
        for (int i = 0; i < elems.length; i++) {
            result.elems[i] = m.apply(elems[i]);
        }
        return result;
    }
}
```

Right:
```java
interface IntMapper {
    public int apply(int v);
}
class IntIncrement implements IntMapper {
    public int apply(int v) {
        return v + 1;
    }
}
```

public class MyArray {

Type: slide, code

Content:
Title: Delegation Chain

Left: Create object
Code:
1. function Counter () { this.n = -1; }
2. Counter.prototype.next = function () {
3.     return this.n += 1;
4. }
5. var c = new Counter ();
6. c.next(); // 0
7. c.next(); // 1
8. c.reset(); // TypeError: c.reset is undefined

Right: Extend delegation chain
Code:
1. function Resettable () { this.reset(); }
2. Resettable.prototype.reset = function () {
3.     this.n = -1;
4. }
5. // Counter "extends" Resettable
6. Counter.prototype.__proto__ = Resettable.prototype
7. c.reset(); // -1
8. c.next(); // 0

Serial Number: 10

Exercise 1
When a function has free variables (i.e., variables that are neither parameters of the function nor local variables in the function body), these free variables must be bound to variables of the function's environment. A closure is a data structure that combines a function with the variables from the environment to make them available on function execution. A common design choice concerns whether the closure should contain copies of the state when the function is defined, or whether it should contain references to memory shared between the closure and the environment. In Scala, the nature of the variable in the environment (mutable vs. immutable) determines this choice: mutable variables (var) are shared, immutable variables (val) are copied. For mutable variables, the closure data structure needs to provide slots for references (e.g., scala.runtime.IntRef); for immutable variables, it needs to provide slots for values (e.g., int).

Resources.
To prepare for this question, revisit
• Slides Closures
• Programming in Scala Chapter 8.7 Closures

Question. Consider the following Scala code:
Code:
def f (x:Int,y:Int) : () => Int = {
  var c = y
  () => {
    c = c + x
  }
}

Top: Exercise 2 — Continuation passing is an implementation style that replaces return values with a continuation function that is invoked with the result. For example, a function in the usual return-value style def f(x: Int) : String that takes an integer and returns a string, is in continuation-passing style def f(x: Int, k: String=>Unit) : Unit.

Resources: Slides Tail Recursion

Question: Consider the following tail-recursive implementation of the factorial function in Scala, using continuation passing:
Code:
def fact (n: Int, k: Int=>Unit) : Unit =
  require (n>=0)
  if n <= 1 then k(1)
  else fact(n-1, resultOfNMinusOne => k(n * resultOfNMinusOne))
end fact

Which of the following continuation functions fits the expected signature of k and prints the result to the console:
A: (x:List[Int]) => println(x)
B: x => ()
C: fact(5, _)
D: (x:Int) => println(x)
E: (x:Int) => x+1

Exercise 5
In Scala, lists can be created by prepending a new head to an existing list using the infix operator ::. This operator is defined in class List, which means that the right-hand side argument must be a list. It is right-associative, so a chain 1 :: 2 :: Nil is equivalent to 1 :: (2 :: Nil). The object Nil is an empty list, Nil == List() is true. Lists can contain any number of homogeneous items, but the Scala type hierarchy allows placing items of different concrete type into one list as long as they share a common base class (in Scala, all types do: scala.Any). The element type of the resulting list is the common base class of the new head and the elements in the existing list. For example, 1 :: List(2, 3) create a List[Int], because the new head is 1:Int and the elements of the existing list are 2:Int and 3:Int.

Exercise 6
Call-by-name in Scala delays evaluation of arguments passed to functions (explicitly requests non-strict argument evaluation instead of the default strict evaluation of function calls). Call-by-name is implemented in Scala as passing parameter-less functions as arguments; such parameter-less functions, by convention, can be called in Scala even when omitting (), so that the resulting code looks as if we were accessing non-strictly evaluated variables.

Resources.
- Slides Argument Passing (Call-By-Name: Scala)
- Programming in Scala Chapter 9.5: By-name parameters

Call-by-name is implemented in Scala as passing parameter-less functions as arguments; such parameter-less functions, by convention, can be called in Scala even when omitting {}, so that the resulting code looks as if we were accessing non-strictly evaluated variables.

Resources.
    • Slides Argument Passing (Call-By-Name: Scala)
    • Programming in Scala Chapter 9.5: By-name parameters

Question. Consider the Scala definitions:
Code:
def f(x: => Int, y: => Int): Int =
    if math.random < 0.5
    then x
    else y
end f

What is the result of evaluating the expression f({println("x");1},{println("y");2}):

A: Prints both x and y, and returns either 1 or 2
B: The expression fails static typechecking because the compound expression {println("x");1} does not return an Int
C: Prints y, and returns either 1 or 2
D: Either prints x and returns 1, or prints y and returns 2
E: Prints x, and returns either 1 or 2

Top: Question. Consider the Scala definitions:

      if math.random < 0.5
      then x
      else y
    end f

What is the result of evaluating the expression f({println("x");1},{println("y");2}):

A: Prints both x and y, and returns either 1 or 2

E: Prints x, and returns either 1 or 2

Solution Strategy.
• Check whether a function argument uses thunk notation, e.g., x : => Int; these arguments are evaluated non-strict only when accessed in the function body

Variations.
• Change def f(x: => Int, y: => Int) to def f(x: Int, y: Int)
• Replace the body of f with x*y

Question: What is the result of evaluating the expression f({println("x");1}, {println("y");2})?

Options:
A: Prints both x and y, and returns either 1 or 2
B: The expression fails static typechecking because the compound expression {println("x");1} does not return an Int
C: Prints y, and returns either 1 or 2
D: Either prints x and returns 1, or prints y and returns 2
E: Prints x, and returns either 1 or 2

Solution Strategy:
• Check whether a function argument uses thunk notation, e.g., x : => Int; these arguments are evaluated non-strict only when accessed in the function body

Variations:
• Change def f(x: => Int, y: => Int) to def f(x: Int, y: Int)
• Replace the body of f with x*y

Type: slide, document

Content:
Top: 
  f({println("x");1}, {println("y");2})
  What is the result of evaluating the expression f({println("x");1}, {println("y");2})?
  A: Prints both x and y, and returns either 1 or 2
  B: The expression fails static typechecking because the compound expression {println("x");1} does not return an Int
  C: Prints y, and returns either 1 or 2
  D: Either prints x and returns 1, or prints y and returns 2
  E: Prints x, and returns either 1 or 2

Middle:
Solution Strategy.
  • Check whether a function argument uses thunk notation, e.g., x : => Int; these arguments are evaluated non-strict only when accessed in the function body

Variations.
  • Change def f(x : => Int, y : => Int) to def f(x: Int, y: Int)
  • Replace the body of f with x*y

B: The expression fails static typechecking because the compound expression {println("x");1} does not return an Int
C: Prints y, and returns either 1 or 2
D: Either prints x and returns 1, or prints y and returns 2
E: Prints x, and returns either 1 or 2

Solution Strategy.
• Check whether a function argument uses thunk notation, e.g., x : => Int; these arguments are evaluated non-strict only when accessed in the function body

Variations.
• Change def f(x: => Int, y: => Int) to def f(x: Int, y: Int)
• Replace the body of f with x*y

Content:
Top: Question. Consider the Scala definitions:
Code: def f(x: => Int, y: => Int): Int =
      if math.random < 0.5
      then x
      else y
    end f

What is the result of evaluating the expression f({println("x");1},{println("y");2}):

A: Prints both x and y, and returns either 1 or 2
B: The expression fails static typechecking because the compound expression {println("x");1} does not return an Int
C: Prints y, and returns either 1 or 2
D: Either prints x and returns 1, or prints y and returns 2
E: Prints x, and returns either 1 or 2

Solution Strategy.
• Check whether a function argument uses thunk notation, e.g., x : => Int; these arguments are evaluated non-strict only when accessed in the function body

Variations.
• Change def f(x: => Int, y: => Int) to def f(x: Int, y: Int)
• Replace the body of f with x*y

D: Either prints x and returns 1, or prints y and returns 2
E: Prints x, and returns either 1 or 2

Solution Strategy.
• Check whether a function argument uses thunk notation, e.g., x : => Int; these arguments are evaluated non-strict only when accessed in the function body

Variations.
• Change def f(x: => Int, y: => Int) to def f(x: Int, y: Int)
• Replace the body of f with x*y

  Exercise 7
  JavaScript uses delegation between objects instead of inheritance between classes. To this end, every object has a field __proto__ pointing to another object that offers functionality for reuse. This field is automatically initialized when using new together with a constructor function that offers a prototype object. JavaScript objects and the links between them can be updated dynamically at runtime.

Content:
Top:
Exercise 7
JavaScript uses delegation between objects instead of inheritance between classes. To this end, every object has a field __proto__ pointing to another object that offers functionality for reuse. This field is automatically initialized when using new together with a constructor function that offers a prototype object. JavaScript objects and the links between them can be updated dynamically at runtime.

Resources.
• Slides Delegation-based OOP
• Eloquent JavaScript: Prototypes

Code:
1 function Box (x) {
2     this.x = x;
3 }
4 Box.prototype.getX = function() { return this.x; }
5
6 let b = new Box(2);
7 console.log(b.getX());
8 b.y = 3;
9
10 let c = new Box(4);
11 console.log(c.getX());
12
13 c.__proto__ = b;
14 console.log(c.y);

• Change b.y = 3; to b.z = 3;
• Remove b.y = 3;
• Change Box.prototype.z = 5; to Box.prototype.y = 5;
• Remove Box.prototype.z = 5;

Center:
8
Serial Number: 10

Bottom:
Exercise 8
JavaScript objects are created from object literals enclosed in {}. This syntax choice is somewhat unfortunate since code blocks are also delimited by {}, so carefully inspect whether braces are blocks of statements or enclose a comma-separated list of key: value pairs. Unlike in other languages, accessing fields and methods from within an object requires this. Whenever we attempt to access a field that is not present in an object, JavaScript returns undefined (sometimes throws exceptions) rather than reporting a compile error.

Question. Consider the following JavaScript code:

Code:
function f () {
  return {
    n: 0,
    get: function () { return this.n; }
  }
}

function g () {
  var n = 0;
  return {
    get: function () { return n; }
  }
}

var f1 = f ();
var g1 = g ();
var g2 = g ();

Identify all of the statements that are true:
1. f1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
2. ... (rest of statements not visible)

  JavaScript objects are created from object literals enclosed in {}. This syntax choice is somewhat unfortunate since code blocks are also delimited by {}, so carefully inspect whether braces are blocks of statements or enclose a comma-separated list of key: value pairs. Unlike in other languages, accessing fields and methods from within an object requires this. Whenever we attempt to access a field that is not present in an object, JavaScript returns undefined (sometimes throws exceptions) rather than reporting a compile error.

Resources.
  • Slides Delegation-Based OOP
  • Eloquent JavaScript: Objects

Code:
function f () {
  return {
    n: 0,
    get: function () { return this.n; }
  }
}

function g () {
  var n = 0;
  return {
    get: function () { return n; }
  }
}

var f1 = f ();

• Every time a function is called, new local variables are placed on the stack and added to closures (if accessed from the returned object)

• Change return this.n in function f to return n

Exercise 9
In object-oriented programming, polymorphism allows us to refer to an object of a subclass through a reference that is statically typed as a base class (upcasting). Polymorphism alone can be used to create generic containers, but puts the burden of reading and writing consistently on programmers. Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

Exercise 9
In object-oriented programming, polymorphism allows us to refer to an object of a subclass through a reference that is statically typed as a base class (upcasting). Polymorphism alone can be used to create generic containers, but puts the burden of reading and writing consistently on programmers. Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

Exercise 9
In object-oriented programming, polymorphism allows us to refer to an object of a subclass through a reference that is statically typed as a base class (upcasting). Polymorphism alone can be used to create generic containers, but puts the burden of reading and writing consistently on programmers. Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

Resources:
• Slides Parametric Polymorphism
• Slides Subtyping
• Programming in Scala Chapter 18 Type Parameterization

class A { override def toString(): String = "A" }
class B extends A { override def toString(): String = "B" }
class C extends B { override def toString(): String = "C" }

The following method uses the classes in containers:
def f () =
  val as: Array[A] = Array(new A(), new A())
  as(0) = new C()
  as(1) = new A()
  println(as.mkString(","))
  
Indicate which one of the following statements is true.

Exercise 9
In object-oriented programming, polymorphism allows us to refer to an object of a subclass through a reference that is statically typed as a base class (upcasting). Polymorphism alone can be used to create generic containers, but puts the burden of reading and writing consistently on programmers. Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

Resources:
• Slides Parametric Polymorphism
• Slides Subtyping
• Programming in Scala Chapter 18 Type Parameterization

In object-oriented programming, polymorphism allows us to refer to an object of a subclass through a reference that is statically typed as a base class (upcasting). Polymorphism alone can be used to create generic containers, but puts the burden of reading and writing consistently on programmers. Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

Resources:
• Slides Parametric Polymorphism
• Slides Subtyping
• Programming in Scala Chapter 18 Type Parameterization

Question:
Consider the following Scala class hierarchy:
class A { override def toString(): String = "A" }
class B extends A { override def toString(): String = "B" }
class C extends B { override def toString(): String = "C" }

The following method uses the classes in containers:
def f () =
  val as: Array[A] = Array(new A(), new A())
  as(0) = new C()
  as(1) = new A()
  println(as.mkString(","))
  
Indicate which one of the following statements is true.
At f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 5.

Question. Consider the following Scala class hierarchy:
class A { override def toString(): String = "A" }
class B extends A { override def toString(): String = "B" }
class C extends B { override def toString(): String = "C" }

The following method uses the classes in containers:

  println(as.mkString(", "))

Indicate which one of the following statements is true.
A: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 5.
B: f passes static typechecking, and prints C,A when executed.
C: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 4.
D: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 3.
E: f passes static typechecking, and prints A,A when executed.

Top: Question. Consider the Scala definitions:
Code: def f(x: => Int, y: => Int): Int =
      if math.random < 0.5
      then x
      else y
    end f

What is the result of evaluating the expression f({println("x");1},{println("y");2}):

A: Prints both x and y, and returns either 1 or 2
B: The expression fails static typechecking because the compound expression {println("x");1} does not return an Int
C: Prints y, and returns either 1 or 2
D: Either prints x and returns 1, or prints y and returns 2
E: Prints x, and returns either 1 or 2

Solution Strategy.
• Check whether a function argument uses thunk notation, e.g., x : => Int; these arguments are evaluated non-strict only when accessed in the function body

Variations.
• Change def f(x: => Int, y: => Int) to def f(x: Int, y: Int)
• Replace the body of f with x*y

class B extends A { override def toString(): String = "B" }
class C extends B { override def toString(): String = "C" }

The following method uses the classes in containers:
def f () =
  val as: Array[A] = Array(new A(), new A())
  as(0) = new C()
  as(1) = new A()
  println(as.mkString(", "))

Indicate which one of the following statements is true.
A: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 5.
B: f passes static typechecking, and prints C,A when executed.
C: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 4.
D: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 3.
E: f passes static typechecking, and prints A,A when executed.

Content:
Exercise 9
In object-oriented programming, polymorphism allows us to refer to an object of a subclass through a reference that is statically typed as a base class (upcasting). Polymorphism alone can be used to create generic containers, but puts the burden of reading and writing consistently on programmers. Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

Question. Consider the following Scala class hierarchy:
class A { override def toString(): String = "A" }
class B extends A { override def toString(): String = "B" }
class C extends B { override def toString(): String = "C" }

The following method uses the classes:
def f () =
  val as: Array[A] = Array(new A, new B, new C)
  as(0) = new C()
  as(1) = new A()
  println(as.mkString(", "))

Indicate which one of the following is correct:
A: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 3.
B: f passes static typechecking, and prints C,A when executed.
C: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 4.
D: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 3.
E: f passes static typechecking, and prints A,A when executed.

Solution Strategy.
• Check that the types of the objects placed into the container are subtypes of the container's type parameter (remember: Array[A] can only contain objects of type A or its subtypes).

C: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 4.
D: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 3.
E: f passes static typechecking, and prints A,A when executed.

Bottom:
Solution Strategy.
• Check that the types of the objects placed into the container are subtypes of the container's type parameter (remember: Array[A] can hold any subtype of A).

Type: slide, code

Content:
Top: Programming in Scala Chapter 18 Type Parameterization

Code:
class A { override def toString(): String = "A" }
class B extends A { override def toString(): String = "B" }
class C extends B { override def toString(): String = "C" }

def f () =
  val as: Array[A] = Array(new A(), new A())
  as(0) = new C()
  as(1) = new A()
  println(as.mkString(", "))

Question: Indicate which one of the following statements is true.
A: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 5.
B: f passes static typechecking, and prints C,A when executed.
C: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 4.
D: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 3.
E: f passes static typechecking, and prints A,A when executed.

Solution Strategy:
• Check that the types of the objects placed into the container are subtypes of the container's type parameter (remember that the subtyping relationship is reflexive A <: A)
• Check that modification of the array respects subtyping relationship: is C <: A, is A <: A?

  • Change val as: Array[A] = Array(new A(), new A()) to val as: Array[B] = Array(null, null)

Exercise 14 In object-oriented programming, subclasses can override inherited methods of their base class with a different implementation. As a result, an object of such a subclass has multiple methods of the same name and signature. A programming language's design chooses how to resolve a method call: static dispatch/lookup/binding (early binding) chooses between the methods at compile time based on the static type of the variable holding the object; dynamic dispatch/lookup/binding (late binding) chooses between the methods at runtime based on the dynamic type of the object itself. C++ uses dynamic dispatch/lookup/binding (late binding) only if both of the following conditions are met: the method must be marked virtual and the variable must be a pointer or reference to the object; if at least one of these conditions is violated, C++ uses static dispatch/lookup/binding.

Resources. To prepare for this question, revisit
- Slides: Dynamic Dispatch and Inheritance

Exercise 9
In object-oriented programming, polymorphism allows us to refer to an object of a subclass through a reference that is statically typed as a base class (upcasting). Polymorphism alone can be used to create generic containers, but puts the burden of reading and writing consistently on programmers. Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

• Slides Subtyping

Exercise 9
In object-oriented programming, polymorphism allows us to refer to an object of a subclass through a reference that is statically typed as a base class (upcasting). Polymorphism alone can be used to create generic containers, but puts the burden of reading and writing consistently on programmers. Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

Resources:
• Slides Parametric Polymorphism
• Slides Subtyping
• Programming in Scala Chapter 18 Type Parameterization

Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

Resources:
• Slides Parametric Polymorphism
• Slides Subtyping
• Programming in Scala Chapter 18 Type Parameterization

Question:
Consider the following Scala class hierarchy:
class A { override def toString(): String = "A" }
class B extends A { override def toString(): String = "B" }
class C extends B { override def toString(): String = "C" }

The following method uses the classes in containers:
def f () =
  val as: Array[A] = Array(new A(), new A())
  as(0) = new C()
  as(1) = new A()
  println(as.mkString(","))
  
Indicate which one of the following statements is true.
At f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 5.

Exercise 9
In object-oriented programming, polymorphism allows us to refer to an object of a subclass through a reference that is statically typed as a base class (upcasting). Polymorphism alone can be used to create generic containers, but puts the burden of reading and writing consistently on programmers. Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

Resources:
• Slides Parametric Polymorphism
• Slides Subtyping
• Programming in Scala Chapter 18 Type Parameterization

Question:
Consider the following Scala class hierarchy:
class A { override def toString(): String = "A" }
class B extends A { override def toString(): String = "B" }
class C extends B { override def toString(): String = "C" }

The following method uses the classes in containers:
def f () =
  val as: Array[A] = Array(new A(), new A())
  as(0) = new C()
  as(1) = new A()
  println(as.mkString(","))
  
Indicate which one of the following statements is true.
At f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 5.

Exercise 9
In object-oriented programming, polymorphism allows us to refer to an object of a subclass through a reference that is statically typed as a base class (upcasting). Polymorphism alone can be used to create generic containers, but puts the burden of reading and writing consistently on programmers. Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

Resources:
• Slides Parametric Polymorphism
• Slides Subtyping
• Programming in Scala Chapter 18 Type Parameterization

Question:
Consider the following Scala class hierarchy:
class A { override def toString(): String = "A" }
class B extends A { override def toString(): String = "B" }
class C extends B { override def toString(): String = "C" }

The following method uses the classes in containers:
def f () =
  val as: Array[A] = Array(new A(), new A())
  as(0) = new C()
  as(1) = new A()
  println(as.mkString(","))
  
Indicate which one of the following statements is true.
At f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 5.

Exercise 9
In object-oriented programming, polymorphism allows us to refer to an object of a subclass through a reference that is statically typed as a base class (upcasting). Polymorphism alone can be used to create generic containers, but puts the burden of reading and writing consistently on programmers. Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

Type parameters add static type information to (container) classes that allow the compiler to check read and write operations for compatibility with the container’s type parameters.

Resources:
• Slides Parametric Polymorphism
• Slides Subtyping
• Programming in Scala Chapter 18 Type Parameterization

Question:
Consider the following Scala class hierarchy:
class A { override def toString(): String = "A" }
class B extends A { override def toString(): String = "B" }
class C extends B { override def toString(): String = "C" }

The following method uses the classes in containers:
def f () =
  val as: Array[A] = Array(new A(), new A())
  as(0) = new C()
  as(1) = new A()
  println(as.mkString(","))
  
Indicate which one of the following statements is true.
At f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 5.

Exercise 28
Variables in a function or code block without a declaration in that block are free variables: in order for the program to compile, free variables must be bound to some binding occurrence (a variable declaration or function argument). In a statically scoped language, binding occurrences are searched in enclosing blocks. Often, closures are formed to align the lifetime of the function that has the variable free with the lifetime of the variable in the binding location.

Resources. To prepare for this question, revisit
• Slides Scope and Lifetime

Exercise 23
In languages with parametric polymorphism, subtyping relationships extend beyond class inheritance relationships. Type covariance, contravariance, and invariance refer to the way how the subtyping relationship between parameterized classes relates to the subtyping relationship of the type parameters. A parameterized type T[.] is covariant if A <: B implies T[A] <: T[B]; for a contravariant type we have A <: B implies T[B] <: T[A]; for an invariant type we have A < B implies T[A] <> T[B] (the types are incomparable). Scala lists are covariant, Scala arrays are invariant. Wildcard class parameters allow us to parameterize with an unknown type of a certain bound: T[? <: A] means we parameterize T with an unknown subtype of A (? <: A). As a result, the elements in T are readable as statically typed A. We cannot modify an instance of T because doing so would require us to create instances of ? (an unknown type).

Resources.
To prepare for this question, revisit
• Slides Subtyping
• Programming in Scala Chapter 18 Type Parameterization

Top: Exercise 19
    Call-by-value languages evaluate function arguments to their values to pass copies of those values to a function. Changes to the copy made inside the called function are invisible to the caller. Call-by-reference languages obtain an L-value of a function argument and pass the l-value (a reference) to a function. Changes made via the reference inside the called function are visible to the caller.

Exercise 16
Algebraic data types, when using recursive type definitions, allow creating tree-like and graph-like object structures that can be easily traversed with a recursive function and pattern matching. In Scala, algebraic data types can be created using enum BaseClass and case SubClass, where the subclasses are allowed to use class parameters of sibling classes and the base class.

Question. Consider the definition f, with nested function g:
Code:
def f [X] (xs:List[X]) : List[List[(X,String)]] = {
  def g (x:X) : List[(X,String)] = {
    xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
  }
  xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
Code:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1–2
C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Question. Consider the definition f, with nested function g:
Code:
def f [X] (xs:List[X]) : List[List[(X,String)]] = {
  def g (x:X) : List[(X,String)] = {
    xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
  }
  xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
Code:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List((1,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1–2
C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Question. Consider the definition f, with nested function g:
Code:
def f [X] (xs:List[X]) : List[List[(X,String)]] = {
  def g (x:X) : List[(X,String)] = {
    xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
  }
  xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
Code:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1–2
C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Solution Strategy.

Question. Consider the definition f, with nested function g:
Code:
def f [X] (xs:List[X]) : List[List[(X,String)]] = {
  def g (x:X) : List[(X,String)] = {
    xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
  }
  xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
Code:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1–2
C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Solution Strategy.

def f [X] (xs:List[X]) : List[List[(X,String)]] = {
  def g (x:X) : List[(X,String)] = {
    xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
  }
  xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
Code:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1–2
C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

    xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
  }
  xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
Code:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1–2
C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

    xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
  }
  xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
Code:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1–2
C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

    xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
  }
  xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
Code:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1–2
C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

  def g(x: X): List[(X, String)] = {
    xs.map ((y: X) => (x, y.toString()))
  }
  xs.map (g)
}
```

Bullet Points:
- Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
- Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
- Combine these partial results into the final result list

Question. Consider the following Scala class hierarchy:
class A { override def toString(): String = "A" }
class B extends A { override def toString(): String = "B" }
class C extends B { override def toString(): String = "C" }

The following method uses the classes in containers:
def f () =
  val as: Array[A] = Array(new A(), new A())
  as(0) = new C()
  as(1) = new A()
  println(as.mkString(", "))

Indicate which one of the following statements is true.
A: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 5.
B: f passes static typechecking, and prints C,A when executed.
C: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 4.
D: f fails static typechecking with a compile error on line 3.
E: f passes static typechecking, and prints A,A when executed.

Question. Consider the definition f, with nested function g:
Code:
def f [X] (xs:List[X]) : List[List[(X,String)]] = {
  def g (x:X) : List[(X,String)] = {
    xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
  }
  xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
Code:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1–2
C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

def f [X] (xs:List[X]) : List[List[(X,String)]] = {
  def g (x:X) : List[(X,String)] = {
    xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
  }
  xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List( (1,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1-2
C: List( List( (1,"1"), (1,"2") ), List( (2,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
D: List( List( (1,"2"), (2,"1") ), List( (1,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
E: List( List( (1,"2"), (2,"1") ) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Variations.
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (y, x.toString()))
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y))

C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Variations.
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (y, x.toString()))
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y))

Top: Exercise 2 — Continuation passing is an implementation style that replaces return values with a continuation function that is invoked with the result. For example, a function in the usual return-value style def f(x: Int) : String that takes an integer and returns a string, is in continuation-passing style def f(x: Int, k: String=>Unit) : Unit.

Resources: Slides Tail Recursion

Question: Consider the following tail-recursive implementation of the factorial function in Scala, using continuation passing:
Code:
def fact (n: Int, k: Int=>Unit) : Unit =
  require (n>=0)
  if n <= 1 then k(1)
  else fact(n-1, resultOfNMinusOne => k(n * resultOfNMinusOne))
end fact

Which of the following continuation functions fits the expected signature of k and prints the result to the console:
A: (x:List[Int]) => println(x)
B: x => ()
C: fact(5, _)
D: (x:Int) => println(x)
E: (x:Int) => x+1

E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Variations.
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (y, x.toString()))
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y))

def f [X] (xs:List[X]) : List[List[(X,String)]] = {
    def g (x:X) : List[(X,String)] = {
        xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
    }
    xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1-2
C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Question. Consider the definition f, with nested function g:
Code:
def f [X] (xs:List[X]) : List[List[(X,String)]] = {
    def g (x:X) : List[(X,String)] = {
        xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
    }
    xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1-2
C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Variations.
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (y, x.toString()))
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y))

For example, a function in the usual return-value style def f(x: Int) : String that takes an integer and returns a string, is in continuation-passing style def f(x: Int, k: String=>Unit) : Unit.

Resources: Slides Tail Recursion

Code:
def fact (n: Int, k: Int=>Unit) : Unit =
  require (n>=0)
  if n <= 1 then k(1)
  else fact(n-1, resultOfNMinusOne => k(n * resultOfNMinusOne))
end fact

Resources: Slides Tail Recursion

Code:
def fact (n: Int, k: Int=>Unit) : Unit =
  require (n>=0)
  if n <= 1 then k(1)
  else fact(n-1, resultOfNMinusOne => k(n * resultOfNMinusOne))
end fact

Resources: Slides Tail Recursion

Question: Consider the following tail-recursive implementation of the factorial function in Scala, using continuation passing:
Code:
def fact (n: Int, k: Int=>Unit) : Unit =
  require (n>=0)
  if n <= 1 then k(1)
  else fact(n-1, resultOfNMinusOne => k(n * resultOfNMinusOne))
end fact

Resources: Slides Tail Recursion

Code:
def fact (n: Int, k: Int=>Unit) : Unit =
  require (n>=0)
  if n <= 1 then k(1)
  else fact(n-1, resultOfNMinusOne => k(n * resultOfNMinusOne))
end fact

Resources: Slides Tail Recursion

Question: Consider the following tail-recursive implementation of the factorial function in Scala, using continuation passing:
Code:
def fact (n: Int, k: Int=>Unit) : Unit =
  require (n>=0)
  if n <= 1 then k(1)
  else fact(n-1, resultOfNMinusOne => k(n * resultOfNMinusOne))
end fact

A: (x:List[Int]) => println(x)
B: x => ()
C: fact(5, _)
D: (x:Int) => println(x)
E: (x:Int) => x+1

Content:
Top: Exercise 24 Mixing side-effecting expressions with arithmetic operations can result in undefined operation sequences, especially when there are multiple assignments to the same variable within a single expression. The expression-sequencing operator (comma ,) can be used to disambiguate the sequence of operations.

Resources: To prepare for this question, revisit
• Slides Undefined Behavior

Code:
int main () {
int x = 1;
x = x + 1;
x = (x++) + 1;
x = (++x) + (x = x*2);
}

Question: Which lines result in an undefined order of operations on variable x?
A: There is no undefined order in the program
B: Only line 3
C: Only line 4
D: Lines 4 and 5
E: Only line 5

Solution Strategy:
• Identify side-effecting expressions: is their evaluation order unambiguous?

Variations:
• Change x = (x++) + 1; to (x++, x=x+1);

• Slides Undefined Behavior

Question. Consider the following C code:
int main () {
int x = 1;
x = x + 1;
x = (x++) + 1;
x = (++x) + (x = x*2);
}

Which lines result in an undefined order of operations on variable x?

D: Lines 4 and 5

• Identify side-effecting expressions: is their evaluation order unambiguous?

Variations.
• Change x = (x++) + 1; to (x++, x=x+1);
• Change x = (++x) + (x = x*2); to (++x, x=x*2, x = x + x);

Question: Consider the following C code:
1 int main () {
2 int x = 1;
3 x = x + 1;
4 x = (x++) + 1;
5 x = (++x) + (x = x*2);
6 }

Which lines result in an undefined order of operations on variable x?
A: There is no undefined order in the program
B: Only line 3
C: Only line 4
D: Lines 4 and 5
E: Only line 5

Solution Strategy:
• Identify side-effecting expressions: is their evaluation order unambiguous?

Variations:
• Change x = (x++) + 1; to (x++, x=x+1);
• Change x = (++x) + (x = x*2); to (++x, x=x*2, x = x + x);

Top: Exercise 23
Text: In languages with parametric polymorphism, subtyping relationships extend beyond class inheritance relationships. Type covariance, contravariance, and invariance refer to the way how the subtyping relationship between parameterized classes relates to the subtyping relationship of the type parameters. A parameterized type T[.] is covariant if A <: B implies T[A] <: T[B]; for a contravariant type we have A <: B implies T[B] <: T[A]; for an invariant type we have A <: B implies T[A] >: T[B] (the types are incomparable). Scala lists are covariant. Scala arrays are invariant. Wildcard class parameters allow us to parameterize with an unknown type of a certain bound: T[? <: A] means we parameterize T with an unknown subtype of A (? <: A). As a result, the elements in T are readable as statically typed A. We cannot modify an instance of T because doing so would require us to create instances of ? (an unknown type).

• Slides Subtyping
• Programming in Scala Chapter 18 Type Parameterization

Exercise 14 In object-oriented programming, subclasses can override inherited methods of their base class with a different implementation. As a result, an object of such a subclass has multiple methods of the same name and signature. A programming language’s design chooses how to resolve a method call: static dispatch/lookup/binding (early binding) chooses between the methods at compile time based on the static type of the variable holding the object; dynamic dispatch/lookup/binding (late binding) chooses between the methods at runtime based on the dynamic type of the object itself. C++ uses dynamic dispatch/lookup/binding (late binding) only if both of the following conditions are met: the method must be marked virtual and the variable must be a pointer or reference to the object; if at least one of these conditions is violated, C++ uses static dispatch/lookup/binding.
