Exercise 11

Summary. The collections processing functions fold, foldLeft, and foldRight turn the elements of a collection into an aggregate result. All three functions use a seed value (like 0 or an empty string) and then "add" element by element to that seed value, but they differ in the order in which elements are processed. Function foldLeft processes elements sequentially, starting from the head of the list; function foldRight processes elements sequentially, starting from the last element of the list. Function fold can process sequentially or in parallel: for sequential processing, fold is equivalent to foldLeft, for parallel processing it applies a divide-and-conquer approach.

Resources. If you find this question challenging, revisit
• Slides "Fold"
• Programming in Scala: Chapter 14.7 (Higher-order methods on class List)

    In object-oriented programming, subclasses can override inherited methods of their base class with a different implementation. As a result, an object of such a subclass has multiple methods of the same name and signature. A programming language's design chooses how to resolve a method call: static dispatch/lookup/binding (early binding) chooses between the methods at compile time based on the static type of the reference pointing to the object; dynamic dispatch/lookup/binding (late binding) chooses between the methods at runtime based on the dynamic type of the object itself.         xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
    }
    xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List((1,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1-2
C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Variations.
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (y, x.toString()))
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y))

Type: slide, code

Content:
Top: Question. Consider the definition f, with nested function g:
Code:
def f [X] (xs:List[X]) : List[List[(X,String)]] = {
  def g (x:X) : List[(X,String)] = {
    xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
  }
  xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List( (1,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1-2
C: List( List( (1,"1"), (1,"2") ), List( (2,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
D: List( List( (1,"2"), (2,"1") ), List( (1,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
E: List( List( (1,"2"), (2,"1") ) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Variations.
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (y, x.toString()))
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y))

Question. Consider the following Scala code:
Code:
class A {
  def f1() = 1
}

class B extends A {
  override def f1() = 5 + super.f1()
  def f2() = 11
}

val x: B = new B()
val y: A = x

print(x.f1())
print(x.f2())
print(y.f1())

What will be printed when the code is executed?
A: 6 11 5
B: 5 11 1
C: 6 11 6
D: 5 11 5
E: 6 11 1

Solution Strategy.
• Determine the static type of variable x and the dynamic type of the object it points to

• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Variations.
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (y, x.toString()))
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List( (1,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1-2
C: List( List( (1,"1"), (1,"2") ), List( (2,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
D: List( List( (1,"2"), (2,"1") ), List( (1,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
E: List( List( (1,"2"), (2,"1") ) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Variations.
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (y, x.toString()))
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y))

Type: slide, code

Content:
Top: Question. Consider the definition f, with nested function g:
Code:
def f [X] (xs:List[X]) : List[List[(X,String)]] = {
  def g (x:X) : List[(X,String)] = {
    xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
  }
  xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List( (1,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1-2
C: List( List( (1,"1"), (1,"2") ), List( (2,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
D: List( List( (1,"2"), (2,"1") ), List( (1,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
E: List( List( (1,"2"), (2,"1") ) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Variations.
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (y, x.toString()))
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y))

• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Variations.
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (y, x.toString()))
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y))

Type: slide, code

Content:
Top: Exercise 10
    In object-oriented programming, subclasses can override inherited methods of their base class with a different implementation. As a result, an object of such a subclass has multiple methods of the same name and signature. A programming language’s design chooses how to resolve a method call: static dispatch/lookup/binding (early binding) chooses between the methods at compile time based on the static type of the reference pointing to the object; dynamic dispatch/lookup/binding (late binding) chooses between the methods at runtime based on the dynamic type of the object itself. Scala uses dynamic dispatch/lookup/binding (late binding). From within the object, the keyword super lets programmers explicitly request that the method inherited from the base class is invoked (instead of the overridden method in the subclass).

Resources:
    • Slides: Dynamic Dispatch and Inheritance
    • Programming in Scala: Chapter 10 Composition and Inheritance

Question: Consider the following Scala code:
Code:
class A {
  def f1() = 1
}

class B extends A {
  override def f1() = 5 + super.f1()
  def f2() = 11
}

val x: B = new B()
val y: A = x

print(x.f1())
print(x.f2())
print(y.f1())

What will be printed when the code is executed?
A: 6 11 5

Code:
class A {
  def f1() = 1
}

class B extends A {
  override def f1() = 5 + super.f1()
  def f2() = 11
}

val x:B = new B()
val y:A = x

print(x.f1())
print(x.f2())
print(y.f1())

Bottom: What will be printed when the code is executed?
A: 6 11 5
B: 5 11 1
C: 6 11 6
D: 5 11 5
E: 6 11 1

Question: Consider the definition f, with nested function g:
Code:
def f [X] (xs:List[X]) : List[List[(X,String)]] = {
    def g (x:X) : List[(X,String)] = {
        xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString()))
    }
    xs.map (g)
}

Consider the expression:
f (List (1, 2))

What is the result of evaluating the above expression?
A: List( List((1,"1"), (2,"2") ) )
B: The program does not compile because String should be X in lines 1-2
C: List( List((1,"1"), (1,"2")), List((2,"1"), (2,"2")) )
D: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")), List((1,"1"), (2,"2")) )
E: List( List((1,"2"), (2,"1")) )

Solution Strategy.
• Turn xs.map (g) into a list of invocations of g(x), one per element of xs
• Then determine the result of each of those g(x)
• Combine these partial results into the final result list

Variations.
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (y, x.toString()))
• Change xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y.toString())) to xs.map ((y:X) => (x, y))

Serial Number: 10

Exercise 1
When a function has free variables (i.e., variables that are neither parameters of the function nor local variables in the function body), these free variables must be bound to variables of the function's environment. A closure is a data structure that combines a function with the variables from the environment to make them available on function execution. A common design choice concerns whether the closure should contain copies of the state when the function is defined, or whether it should contain references to memory shared between the closure and the environment. In Scala, the nature of the variable in the environment (mutable vs. immutable) determines this choice: mutable variables (var) are shared, immutable variables (val) are copied. For mutable variables, the closure data structure needs to provide slots for references (e.g., scala.runtime.IntRef); for immutable variables, it needs to provide slots for values (e.g., int).

Resources.
To prepare for this question, revisit
• Slides Closures
• Programming in Scala Chapter 8.7 Closures

Question. Consider the following Scala code:
Code:
def f (x:Int,y:Int) : () => Int = {
  var c = y
  () => {
    c = c + x
  }
}

public class MyGUI extends Frame {
    private int count = 0;

    public MyGUI() {
        setSize(200, 100);
        setLayout(new FlowLayout());

        Button button = new Button("Go"); add(button);
        Label out = new Label("000", Label.CENTER); add(out);

        // functional interface: uses closure for count/this and out

            count += 1;
            out.setText(String.format("%03d", count));

}

时间戳: 03:13:39 (11619.00s), OCR耗时: 1.95s, 平均耗时: 1.89s, InputTokens: 1397, OutputTokens: 219
============================================================
Type: code

Content:
```
xs = ["10", "10", "10"];
xs.map(parseInt) /* [10, NaN, 2] */ ... why!?

• Array.map passes three arguments to its callback: (element, index, array).
parseInt accepts two: (string, radix).

So what actually executes is:
parseInt("10", 0)  // radix 0 → treated as base 10 → 10
parseInt("10", 1)  // radix 1 → invalid          → NaN
parseInt("10", 2)  // radix 2 → binary "10"     → 2

Fix: Wrap it so only the element is passed:
xs.map(x => parseInt(x, 10))  // [10, 10, 10]

Or use Number:
xs.map(Number)  // [10, 10, 10] - Number only takes one arg anyway

※ Churned for 7s
```
